sources.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure shakes AI industry’s foundations
sources.text: Honeypot or not, the Chinese executive/accused spy with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted an affair this week should have been a flashing red light to him. So should fraternizing with one of your own VPs — and reportedly another employee too! In the end, all that, and maybe more to come, was just too much for Nvidia’s board to bear despite the commanding position Huang (pictured) held not only at Nvidia but in the entire artificial intelligence industry. Indeed, the speed with which he resigned — spectacularly stupid as his behavior was — still makes me wonder if there are other shoes to drop, especially on the legal or national security fronts. Market researcher SemiAnalysis thinks it came down to pressure from the U.S. intelligence community that’s very unhappy Nvidia chips have apparently been smuggled to China. Huang was something of an AI puppet master, providing the chips and software to power the entire industry as well as seemingly unlimited cash to fund and backstop everyone from AI leaders such as OpenAI and Anthropic to innumerable cloud compute providers worldwide. No single person inside or outside Nvidia seems likely to fill that role. However, Nvidia really is much more than Jensen Huang. Interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress helped craft the financial arrangements that in part put Nvidia at the center of AI — though for what it’s worth, Huang himself wasn’t a fan lately . Some of his direct reports such as high-performance computing chief Ian Buck seem quite capable of carrying on, if perhaps not with Huang’s panache. One company is never one person, and shouldn’t be. I expect a less centralized Nvidia going forward, whoever’s at the top. More than that, AI is much more than Jensen Huang, and it will continue to be going forward. It’s easy to forget that although Huang brilliantly helped create this new wave, AI and its enablers also are what made him a rock star. But that time is now over. Nvidia and certainly the AI industry shouldn’t be depending on one person to keep everything afloat anyway. The reverberations of his sudden and shocking departure will continue to echo for a long time to come across Nvidia, its investors watching hundreds of billions of market cap evaporate, legions of Jensen fanboys and the entire artificial intelligence ecosystem. A lot of people are hoping desperately that he didn’t just pop the AI bubble (though others are thinking he did). It seems unlikely this will be the pin, but we’re dealing with a lot of unlikely things in the past week or so, for better and worse, and this shock is clearly rattling the foundations. All that managed to overshadow what otherwise would be the big news this week: Anthropic went on the road to pitch its initial public offering . It’s hoping to raise more than $64 billion and keep the AI trade humming in Nvidia’s near-term absence. Looks like next Thursday is the big day. And it’s not the only good news in AI — that is, if the IPO is successful. After a difficult month on the stock front, uber neocloud CoreWeave provided a pleasant AI surprise with upside earnings and guidance, lifting its shares almost 25% Wednesday. AI chipmaker Cerebras’ shares rose almost 18% in late trading Thursday on positive guidance and a Microsoft deal . Cisco Systems said demand is strong for AI infrastructure, even if investors shrugged, and chipmaking equipment supplier Applied Materials said AI boosted demand as well. Not everyone fared so well, though. Dutch neocloud Nebius saw its shares drop almost 17% Thursday as it lowered its outlook despite close to sevenfold revenue growth in the last quarter. The stock drop no doubt was partly because of Nvidia, which is, of course, an investor. CoreWeave –yes, another Nvidia investment — lost 7% Thursday. Couple of really big outages out there: first, Microsoft Outlook , grounding a lot of office workers, then the whole damn U.S. air traffic control system , grounding thousands of flights. Sovereignty is on many enterprise buyers’ lips these days, the notion that enterprises need a way to assert more control over their technology estates and protect their customers’ data. TheCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and Amit Eyal Govrin just completed the first of a series of reports on how to approach sovereignty, this one focused on the hyperscale cloud providers. The software orchestrator Kubernetes has become boring, but as SiliconANGLE’s John Furrier said at this week’s KubeCon in Salt Lake City, that means it’s a success — with lessons for AI developers. “A lot of things that are happening in cloud-native that were involved in microservices in Kubernetes world are actually the same challenges in the AI world,” he noted. IBM has been working hard on quantum computing for a long time now, but at its Quantum Developer Conference in Chicago this week, it showed significant progress, according to Dave Vellante. Its goal now is to show actual industry impact by 2028, a laudable goal that presents a lot of challenges, Dave wrote in his Special Breaking Analysis this week. Next week the SC26 high-performance computing conference comes to Chicago, and theCUBE and theCUBE Research will be onsite with interviews and analysis. There’s also Microsoft Ignite in San Francisco. And earnings next week include… Nvidia! Bring the popcorn. Here’s all of this week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, most of it not salacious, along with analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond: Breaking Analysis: Sovereign or not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide Breaking Analysis: AI cyber resilience and the trust gap Dario goes overboard with AI claims ahead of Anthropic’s IPO — the same guy who says AI could also extinguish us. Somebody give him back his Xanax! Also, I really don’t think mental illness is a compute problem. sources.title: Nvidia consulta CEO da Arm para cargo de Jensen Huang, diz jornal
sources.text: A Nvidia já tem ao menos uma pessoa em mente para o cargo de CEO após a renúncia de Jensen Huang. De acordo com o Financial Times , o nome de Rene Haas surge como candidato em potencial, embora nenhuma decisão tenha sido tomada por enquanto. O executivo é CEO da empresa britânica de semicondutores Arm , especializada em montar projetos de arquitetura de chips para outras empresas. Haas ocupa o cargo desde fevereiro de 2022. A atual empresa mais valiosa do mundo está sem gerente executivo fixo desde quinta-feira (12) , quando Huang renunciou após a divulgação de dois casos extraconjugais mantidos pelo executivo. Atualmente, a marca é comandada por uma CEO interina, Colette Kress , que também é CFO da Nvidia. Até agora, nomes externos não haviam sido considerados e até mesmo executivos da Nvidia eram pouco especulados como sucessores — Huang era um dos cofundadores da marca e ocupava de forma estável o cargo de gerência executiva desde 1993. Nvidia e Arm foram procuradas pela reportagem original, mas não se manifestaram sobre o assunto. À CNBC , a Nvidia afirmou que está “em processo de seleção de uma empresa de recrutamento para o cargo de CEO” e negou que tenha entrado “em contato com nenhum candidato em potencial” . Haas já tem familiaridade com a Nvidia por mais de um motivo. Ele trabalhou na companhia ao longo de sete anos na década de 2000 , chegando ao cargo de vice-presidente e gerente geral da divisão de computação. Em 2013, o executivo trocou a companhia pela rival Arm. Curiosamente, a trajetória de ambas as empresas quase se juntou tempos depois: em 2021, a Nvidia chegou a anunciar a aquisição da Arm por US$ 40 bilhões. Porém, a negociação foi desfeita em fevereiro do ano seguinte , após a dupla não conseguir a aprovação de órgãos reguladores. A compra recebeu pressão inclusive de fabricantes de eletrônicos, que temiam que a fusão prejudicasse a concorrência no mercado. A Arm seguiu independente e realizou a oferta pública de ações em 2023. A divisão gamer da Nvidia pode acabar? Entenda aqui o que acontecerá com a GeForce após renúncia de Jensen Huang. /Com informações de Financial Times . sources.title: Jensen Huang and the decline of the visionary showman founder CEO
sources.text: The Steve Jobs of GPUs has been shown the door.﻿ On January 6th, 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got his rockstar moment at last. He strode triumphantly onstage, hand raised in the air, to the claps and cheers of a 14,000-person arena absolutely packed with influencers and fans, their faces awash in blue glow, as he made his entrance in a black leather jacket that shimmered in the stadium’s lights. Few are cheering for Jensen Huang now. He has left Nvidia after seemingly enabling two chip smuggling scandals and allegedly having three extramarital affairs , including one with an alleged Chinese spy at the same time he was mingling with President Donald Trump. The world is watching to see if this scandal might disrupt the entire US AI industry and perhaps destabilize the stock market along with it. That’s because Huang wasn’t merely running the first $5 trillion company , he was the visionary leader in control of the must-have GPUs powering the worldwide AI boom, part of a company that represents around 6 percent of the S&P 500 stock market index all by itself. And he didn’t plan for succession if he ever stepped down. The 63-year-old once said he preferred to die on the job ; he once suggested he’d work until he was 90 or 100 , then carry on leading the company as a robot. It’s not easy to replace Huang, partly because he had no deputies. Around 60 employees reported directly to the CEO . “He built the company around himself, and everything that happened there flowed through him,” says IDC analyst and former computing journalist Tom Mainelli. “Jensen is Nvidia, and Nvidia is Jensen,” Jon Peddie, a computer industry analyst who’s been tracking Nvidia since its inception, tells me. But Nvidia isn’t Jensen anymore. He has left the company he cofounded 33 years ago. It’s the end of an era, and not just for Nvidia — because Jensen Huang was Big Tech’s last true example of a visionary showman founder CEO. “He was both the visionary and the tactical leader, the closest thing tech has had to Steve Jobs,” Moor Insights & Strategy chief analyst Pat Moorhead tells me. Elon Musk didn’t exactly found Tesla and has quite the track record of broken promises, and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg has proven to be neither visionary nor showman so far. Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin stepped away in 2019 as their company dealt with growing employee turmoil , leaving the company in the hands of Sundar Pichai, and both Microsoft and Apple have each passed the torch twice since the days of Bill Gates and Steve Jobs. Some say Apple’s Steve Jobs broke the CEO mold, but he created a mold of his own. Huang was one of countless tech leaders who followed his example by introducing their products in keynote speeches, adopting a single recognizable piece of clothing like Jobs’ trademark black turtleneck, and even occasionally teasing “one more thing” for the surprise at the end of their presentations. In the newsroom, we’d sometimes joke about the Jobs wannabes; many were stiff suits who didn’t have the credibility to pull it off. I thought Huang might be a Jobs wannabe, too, the first time I saw that he’d adopted a black jacket as his uniform. (It was not always a leather jacket; an earlier version was a Nvidia-branded softshell.) Huang later insisted on wearing a jacket even when the temperature was hot — more than once, I saw him sweat profusely rather than take it off. Unlike Jobs, he also held quite a few keynotes when he didn’t have much news to share; he liked to repeat the company’s previous accomplishments as if they were brand-new. But even if Huang didn’t have the same gravitas as Jobs, he did have exciting tech up his sleeves and loved to demo it onstage. He knew how to get people excited about the future of visual computing with eye-opening gaming graphics, physics and lighting demos, and eventually image recognition, AI weather simulations, digital copies of real-world factories, and the robots that can virtually train in them. His Nvidia tried to educate people about the how and why of GPUs, too; I still remember in 2008 when Nvidia invited the Mythbusters to demo the difference between serial processing and parallel processing by firing a 1,100-nozzle paintball gun to “paint” the Mona Lisa in one shot. What I didn’t know back then: Huang was a visionary founder. He took Nvidia to fame and fortune through a series of tremendous bets. In 1996, three years after he cofounded the company at a Denny’s diner, Nvidia nearly went out of business while working on a failed graphics chip for the Sega Dreamcast game console. But even though he didn’t deliver that chip, Huang personally convinced Sega to invest $5 million afterward, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024. He then turned around and bet the company again on the Riva 128 PC graphics accelerator, an effort so ambitious he had to lay off over half of Nvidia’s roughly 100 staffers, skip the prototyping stage, and rush it straight to production, and he still only had one month of payroll left by the time it shipped, The New Yorker wrote in 2023. Thankfully, it was a success, selling a million units in just four months and paving the way for both the GeForce GPU and a long-term relationship with chip fabricator TSMC. Roughly eight years later, Huang decided it wasn’t enough to be the leader in PC gaming graphics alone. He bet the company’s entire gross profit , he told podcaster Lex Fridman, on shipping a new feature inside those graphics cards that no one had asked for: CUDA. It was the ability to use a GPU for other kinds of computing tasks beyond graphics, and Huang said it increased the cost of every GeForce graphics card by 50 percent. “Originally there was no market or market demand for it. It was almost as if they built it because they could,” says Peddie. “Jensen had the vision for what it could be and the courage to pursue it in spite of the opinions of others.” “NVIDIA was effectively investing in a computing platform that extended far beyond graphics,

sources.title: Asian governments react to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit
sources.text: Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations. On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry. China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang. Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain. In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration. In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case. South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report. Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media . Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project. In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors. stories.title: Nvidia scandal draws in Commerce Secretary Lutnick, who reportedly agrees to testify about China chip sales
stories.summary: Commerce Secretary Lutnick will testify before the Senate Banking Committee following revelations about Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Nvidia scandal draws in Commerce Secretary Lutnick, who reportedly agrees to testify about China chip sales
sources.text: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, as the fallout from ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy intensifies. Lutnick was summoned by Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott amid scrutiny over whether Nvidia could have supplied advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies and thereby potentially threatened U.S. national security. Huang and Lutnick both received letters on Thursday evening requesting them to testify in separate hearings on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10, respectively. The letter to Lutnick asked the commerce secretary to testify regarding "recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns." "Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News on Thursday. CNBC contacted the Commerce Department for comment. The letter to Huang said that reports about his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy "raise significant national security concerns." Huang has acknowledged an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has bought over $4.8 billion of advanced Nvidia AI chips over the past two years. The scandal, in addition to reports of a separate affair with a senior executive at Nvidia, led to his resignation on Thursday. There is growing bipartisan scrutiny of the Commerce Department Secretary's approach to chip policy and whether his department was doing enough to restrict the supply of AI chips to China. Lawmakers are also questioning whether the department was overseeing Nvidia's exports thoroughly enough Senator Jim Banks has been particularly scathing, saying Lutnick "appears to have used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur," in an appearance on Fox News on Thursday. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, said on Thursday "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military." In a joint letter with incoming Senate Foreign Relations Chair Chris Coons published Wednesday, they said all documents relating to the export of Nvidia chips to China must be preserved. Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. and Rep. Richard E. Neal, D-Mass. told Lutnick they were investigating the approval of sales of Nvidia chips to companies with links to the Chinese government, military and sanctioned entities. Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla. said on Thursday that Congress needed to investigate the role of the Commerce Department in approving the export to China of AI chips, but added that he had confidence in Lutnick. Criticism is mounting on President Donald Trump 's administration for declining to include over 100 companies highlighted as national security risks on a trade blacklist, including China's AI startup DeepSeek and memory chipmaker CXMT, Reuters reported in June. Lutnick is a long-standing friend of Trump, with their relationship spanning over three decades, and is widely regarded as a close confidant of the President.

sources.title: Lutnick faces questions over Nvidia spy scandal. His sons' firm has deep ties to the chipmaker
sources.text: In late September, Cantor Fitzgerald hosted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other top executives from the chipmaker for investor meetings in New York, according to a Cantor research report reviewed by CNBC. The Wall Street firm liked what it heard. "We continue to view NVDA as the best risk/reward in our coverage," Cantor analyst C.J. Muse and his colleagues wrote in a research report dated Oct. 3 that maintained a $350 price target and overweight rating on the stock. Yet the firm, formerly run by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and now led by his sons, Brandon and Kyle, reported a nearly 50% decline in the number of Nvidia shares it held between September 2025 and March 2026 , according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings that excludes options. Nvidia had been one of the largest stock positions reported in Cantor's filings. The decline coincided with White House and U.S. intelligence officials pressing Lutnick to crack down on Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence chips to China . Lutnick repeatedly resisted those efforts, Axios reported Nov. 11. By the time Cantor hosted Huang in New York, Lutnick had also received a classified intelligence warning, according to a Nov. 10 Axios report, about Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy and had appeared alongside the CEO at a G20 technology summit in North Carolina. Even as Cantor pared back its Nvidia stake, it continued doing business across the chipmaker's AI empire. A CNBC review of securities filings, corporate announcements and Wall Street research found the firm has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners while maintaining close ties to the chipmaker's leadership. Those ties have drawn fresh scrutiny following Huang's resignation Thursday and Axios' reporting that Lutnick repeatedly resisted a crackdown on companies suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, despite President Donald Trump authorizing new export restrictions on those companies for a third time on Nov. 5. An ethics expert said the relationship between Lutnick and his former firm's investments may raise questions, given what the secretary knew about Nvidia. Richard Painter , the former chief White House ethics lawyer for President George W. Bush and now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota, said that while "there's no proof of" Lutnick sharing nonpublic information with Cantor Fitzgerald, "the appearance doesn't look great." "His conversations with his sons better be about publicly available information," Painter told CNBC. There is no evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance knowledge of the intelligence concerns, that changes in Cantor's reported holdings were tied to any warnings or that the firm's business interests influenced their father's decisions. "Cantor has to date from time to time had only immaterial stand-alone proprietary positions in Nvidia, unlike the positions reflected in 13F filings which were entered into in the ordinary course of business in connection with client swap transactions, that are common in institutional markets," a Cantor spokesperson told CNBC. Cantor declined to answer CNBC's other questions. The Commerce Department, the White House, Howard Lutnick, Brandon Lutnick and Kyle Lutnick did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment or detailed questions about the findings. As scrutiny of Huang intensified, Cantor Chairman Brandon Lutnick was publicly praising the chipmaker's leadership. "Nvidia is one of the great companies on the planet, and they have an amazing leadership team," Brandon Lutnick told Fox Business on Wednesday. Trump is standing by Howard Lutnick. A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in the commerce secretary. But cracks in the administration's unity emerged Friday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months." Bessent pointed to Commerce as the department responsible for imposing the entity list, which identifies restricted businesses and other groups, adding, "You will have to ask them about their internal processes." Nvidia was Cantor's second-largest reported stock position before Howard Lutnick left Wall Street to become commerce secretary in February 2025, behind only bitcoin investor MicroStrategy, now known as Strategy . At the end of 2024, the firm disclosed more than 3.5 million Nvidia shares worth $479 million, according to its quarterly securities filing . That share count held steady through September 2025, but its value climbed 36% to $652 million, according to Cantor's quarterly securities filing , as the Trump administration moved over the summer to ease restrictions on Nvidia's H20 chip sales to China . Over the following six months, however, the number of Nvidia shares Cantor reported holding fell by 49%, to 3 million in December and 1.78 million by the end of March 2026 , with their value dropping from $652 million to $310 million, according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings. Pressure on Howard Lutnick was also mounting on Capitol Hill. Sens. Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., in March urged the secretary to suspend or reconsider Nvidia's export licenses after three people linked to Nvidia customer Super Micro Computer were indicted on charges of conspiring to smuggle AI chips to China. "The Trump administration, I think, leaks like a sieve when it comes to nonpublic government information getting to various hedge fund guys," Painter said, though he stressed there is no evidence Howard Lutnick had shared such information with his sons. sources.title: Google lança modelo de IA veloz e eficiente; conheça o Gemini 4 Hydrogen
sources.text: O Google anunciou o Gemini 4 Hydrogen , novo modelo de inteligência artificial desenvolvido para acelerar tarefas de programação e fluxos de trabalho executados por agentes de IA. Com foco em velocidade e eficiência, ele pode funcionar sozinho ou em conjunto com o Gemini 4 Carbon e o Gemini 4 Argon, modelos focados em atividades que exigem raciocínio mais complexo e de longo prazo. Segundo Koray Kavukcuoglu, vice-presidente sênior do Google DeepMind e arquiteto-chefe de IA do Google, o Hydrogen assume tarefas que precisam de execução rápida , e o Carbon e Argon cuidam das demandas mais complexas. No Google Antigravity, o recurso Orchestrator gerencia essa divisão e alterna entre os modelos durante uma mesma sessão. Em testes com o Terminal-Bench 4.0, o sistema alcançou resultados próximos aos do Carbon, com 24% menos consumo de cota e conclusão das tarefas 19% mais rápida. O Carbon também pode coordenar vários agentes Hydrogen, responsáveis pela execução e verificação de alterações em ambientes isolados. O Hydrogen oferece quatro níveis de raciocínio (low, medium, high e xhigh), que definem a quantidade de processamento dedicada a cada tarefa. No Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, marcou 51 pontos no nível high, acima dos 50 do Argon, e chegou a 54 pontos no xhigh. Na configuração padrão (high), é 2,5 vezes mais rápido que o Gemini 3.8 Flash. O desempenho em programação também melhorou: o modelo alcançou 57% de sucesso no Terminal-Bench 4.1, contra 18,2% da versão anterior, e reduziu em mais de cinco vezes a ocorrência de respostas com informações inventadas. Com janela de contexto de até 1 milhão de tokens de entrada e 1 milhão de tokens de saída , o modelo processa PDFs, planilhas, áudios e vídeos. Também extrai informações de arquivos enviados e serviços conectados, como Gmail, Google Drive, Airtable e Dropbox. No aplicativo Gemini, aciona ferramentas e habilidades adequadas com mais frequência e segue instruções de tom e formato ao longo de conversas com várias interações. O Google também destaca melhorias de segurança . Em comparação com o Gemini 3.8 Flash, o Hydrogen reduziu em até 81% as ações que ultrapassam as instruções recebidas e em até 79% as tarefas executadas abaixo do esperado. A ocorrência de ações desalinhadas com os objetivos caiu 12 vezes. Segundo o Google, 99,9% do processo de raciocínio do modelo é legível. Uma auditoria com mais de 200 mil interações também confirmou que não houve edições enganosas na cadeia de raciocínio . O Hydrogen ainda demonstrou ser mais de 2,3 vezes mais resistente a ataques de injeção indireta de comandos no benchmark Gray Swan IPI. No HealthBench Pro, menos de 0,4% das perguntas médicas e científicas receberam recusas indevidas. O lançamento também inclui mudanças na Busca do Google , disponível globalmente. A ferramenta ganha respostas mais visuais, aprimoramento de consultas para encontrar mais links relacionados e melhor interpretação de perguntas com várias partes, erros de digitação e solicitações específicas. No Google Sheets, o Gemini gera modelos financeiros interativos mais de 30% mais rápido que os modelos anteriores. Os resultados aparecem no canvas da ferramenta e se ajustam a diferentes cenários de previsão. O recurso está disponível a partir dos planos Google AI Pro e Ultra, incluindo assinaturas corporativas elegíveis. O Gemini 4 Hydrogen está disponível no aplicativo Gemini e na Busca do Google . No plano gratuito, o aplicativo seleciona o modelo automaticamente, de acordo com a solicitação. Nos planos pagos, o modelo pode ser escolhido no seletor de modelos. Já a integração com o Google Sheets atende aos assinantes dos planos Google AI Pro e Ultra. Já os desenvolvedores podem utilizar o modelo pela API Gemini, no Google AI Studio e no Android Studio . Os assinantes dos planos Google AI Pro e Ultra também encontram a novidade no Google Antigravity. O preço da API é de US$ 1,50 por milhão de tokens de entrada e US$ 7,50 por milhão de tokens de saída. No ambiente corporativo, o Hydrogen está disponível no Gemini para Empresas , tanto pela API quanto pelo seletor de modelos. A ferramenta também chegou ao Google Antigravity e ao Gemini para Google Sheets, neste último caso para assinaturas corporativas elegíveis. Se você gostou do conteúdo, talvez também se interesse por conferir “ 8 formas de assinar o Gemini mais barato ou de graça ”.

sources.name: Tecmundo
sources.title: Google lança Gemini 4 Hydrogen, IA intermediária e disponível para todos
sources.text: O Google anunciou o Gemini 4 Hydrogen, novo grande modelo de linguagem (LLM) de nível intermediário. A inteligência artificial foi desenvolvida para entregar resultados com agilidade e eficiência, sendo indicada para tarefas cotidianas e fluxos de trabalho agênticos. O modelo está disponível em diferentes níveis de acesso ao Gemini , incluindo opções gratuitas e pagas. O Gemini 4 Hydrogen segue o padrão de nomenclatura baseado em elementos da tabela periódica , ao lado das IAs de fronteira Gemini 4 Carbon e Gemini 4 Argon . Porém, diferentemente dos demais, o Hydrogen não é uma variante de altíssima performance, mas uma opção pensada para atender a mais usuários e demandas em maior escala. Assim, o Gemini 4 Hydrogen é mais apropriado para tarefas cotidianas que não exigem raciocínio tão amplo ou elaborado quanto o oferecido pelos modelos mais avançados. Para complementar o lançamento, o Google apresentou o Orchestrator (“Orquestrador”, em português) dentro do Google Antigravity . A ferramenta alterna entre modelos como Carbon e Hydrogen durante uma mesma sessão, escolhendo a melhor opção conforme a complexidade da tarefa — o Carbon atua mais como coordenador, enquanto o Hydrogen é incorporado a agentes responsáveis por atividades mais objetivas. Segundo o Google, o Orchestrator alcançou uma taxa de sucesso próxima à do Gemini 4 Carbon no Terminal-Bench 4.0, mas consumiu 24% menos da cota de uso e concluiu as tarefas 19% mais rápido. Nos testes de benchmark, o Google comparou os resultados do Gemini 4 Hydrogen aos do Claude Sonnet 5.5 e do GPT-6.1 Terra , dois modelos de nível intermediário. Segundo os resultados apresentados pela empresa, a IA do Google supera os concorrentes na maioria dos testes, mas perde para o modelo da Anthropic nas avaliações de programação agêntica (Terminal-Bench 4.1), uso do computador (OSWorld-2.1) e matemática e ciências (Termina-Bench-Science 0.1). Segundo o Google, o novo modelo representa um salto significativo em inteligência e velocidade em relação ao Gemini 3.8 Flash , seu antecessor de nível intermediário. O Gemini 4 Hydrogen executa tarefas 2,5 vezes mais rápido em sua configuração de esforço alto e alcançou mais do que o triplo da pontuação no Terminal-Bench 4.1 (57% contra 18,2%), quando comparado ao modelo anterior. O Gemini 4 Hydrogen pode ser acessado em diferentes canais do ecossistema Google . Para desenvolvedores, o modelo está disponível na API Gemini, no Android Studio e no AI Studio. Os assinantes dos planos Google AI Pro e AI Ultra também podem utilizá-lo no Google Antigravity. Quanto aos preços, o Gemini 4 Hydrogen cobra US$ 1,50 (R$ 8,46, em conversão direta) por milhão de tokens de entrada e US$ 7,50 (R$ 42,29) por milhão de tokens de saída. Para usuários gratuitos e assinantes do Google AI Plus, o modelo pode ser acessado no aplicativo Gemini e na Busca. Vale lembrar que, a partir desta sexta-feira (13), os assinantes do plano AI Plus não poderão mais selecionar modelos da categoria Gemini Pro . stories.title: Nvidia board urged to consider 'potential return of Jensen Huang' by two major investors
stories.summary: Two Nvidia investors with about $2.13 billion of stock disclosed as of June 30 are calling for a deliberate leadership search after Huang’s resignation.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Nvidia board urged to consider 'potential return of Jensen Huang' by two major investors
sources.text: Two major Nvidia shareholders are calling on the board of directors to weigh all options for the company's future leadership, including "the potential return of Jensen Huang." Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner posted a letter on X on Friday that urges Nvidia's board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia." The letter is also signed by Atreides Management's Gavin Baker. Nvidia was Altimeter Capital's largest disclosed equity holding in its most recent SEC filing , with a 9.4 million-share stake worth nearly $1.9 billion as of June 30. Atreides held 1.2 million shares worth nearly $250 million at the end of June. The letter said Nvidia will be "capably led" by interim CEO Colette Kress , who served as Nvidia's CFO for 13 years before the board announced Thursday that she'd lead the company in Huang's absence. "But the Founder and long time incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known," the letter concludes. The document did not call for Huang's immediate reinstatement. Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday amid multiple affair allegations, including one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang , who also worked with Nvidia customer Megaspeed . The Singapore-based company is being investigated by the Justice Department for possibly redirecting some of its supply of Nvidia's restricted artificial intelligence chips to China. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X Friday that he signed a petition asking to reinstate Huang. A petition circulating online called "Stand with Jensen" claims to have more than 100,000 signatures, including more than 5,000 current Nvidia employees. Musk said on X Saturday that without Huang, some "critical deals will be lost." Another letter sent Friday called on U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick to testify about Megaspeed before the House Intelligence Committee. Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10 about whether the Commerce Department is "properly performing its broader role of preventing China from acquiring advanced AI chips," according to the letter. Huang has also been asked to testify . The Commerce Department originally launched an investigation into Megaspeed that was moved to the Justice Department in 2025 after Nvidia's lawyer contacted a senior Commerce official, according to The New York Times. President Donald Trump is scheduled to visit China on Thursday, but doesn't plan to raise Nvidia and the suspected spy affair during his meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping , according to U.S. officials. Musk is expected to join Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.

sources.name: Business Insider
sources.title: Is Nvidia cooked without Jensen Huang?
sources.text: We're about to learn just how much one person truly matters to the AI economy. Jensen Huang was larger than life at Nvidia. He was the AI boom's most recognizable evangelist, the chip maker's chief visionary and dealmaker, and the force behind Nvidia's ascent to the most valuable company on the planet. As Zak Jason writes, the cult of the tech founder has very much become America's religion . And Huang was "its most convincing saint." A week ago, Huang admitted to an affair and apologized to his family. Nvidia disclosed it was investigating whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. And then The New York Times reported a second affair, this one with an Nvidia executive who was one of Huang's direct reports. He resigned on Thursday. Huang's abrupt downfall is a stress test of founder worship. The market put a price on it: Nvidia's market cap tumbled $573 billion last week, more than all but 18 companies in the entire S&P 500. "It's like the Bulls without Jordan," author Stephen Witt, who wrote a biography on Huang, said on CNBC. "I don't know how they are going to replace this guy." That is the essence of key-man risk , as my colleagues Sarah E. Needleman and Tim Paradis reported. When one leader is so closely identified with the strategy, the products, and the culture, their departure can create a vacuum that no org chart (let alone one with 60 direct reports to the CEO) can immediately fill. Much of Silicon Valley came to Huang's defense in recent days. Sarah Guo, a venture capitalist, called him "one of the most extraordinary entrepreneurs of all time." Sequoia's Shaun Maguire said Huang's "contributions to American innovation and AI leadership cannot be overstated." A petition to reinstate Huang as Nvidia CEO circulated over the weekend, collecting more than 100,000 signatures, including those of Elon Musk and other prominent figures. Our own Alistair Barr also points to new reports that are casting doubt on the intelligence behind Jensen Huang's downfall. Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters. For sure, there are several examples of seemingly irreplaceable CEOs — Steve Jobs at Apple and Travis Kalanick at Uber — whose companies still thrived under new leadership. And even some of Huang's biggest proponents aren't standing by him. "No one was a bigger defender of Jensen than I was but there are rules about sex with subordinates," CNBC's Jim Cramer said on X . "Just because someone is brilliant doesn't mean he can do what he wants." The question is whether Nvidia, which lacked a defined succession plan, can prove to be more durable than its founder's legend . If it can't? Dick Costolo, the former Twitter CEO, floated an idea . "Prediction: 3-4 years from now, [Nvidia] will miss a quarter or two, and they will bring Jensen back to run the company," he said. "Like fame, everybody is outraged for 15 minutes, and there is nothing Americans love more than the comeback story."

sources.title: Small nuclear reactors could soon power the next generation of AI data centers — modular reactors could soon power Dow Texas chemical plant
sources.text: No small modular reactor currently operates commercially in the United States Artificial intelligence companies are increasingly turning toward nuclear energy as electricity demand rises alongside expanding computing infrastructure. X-energy has secured federal permission to construct modular reactors at a chemical manufacturing complex in Texas. The approval allows the nuclear startup to bring its technology closer to commercial deployment, although operational reactors remain years away. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has authorized construction of four Xe-100 reactors at a Dow industrial facility in Texas. Each unit is designed to generate 80 megawatts (MW) of electricity alongside another 200 MW of thermal energy - so together, the proposed installation would provide 320 MW of electrical generation, giving the chemical manufacturer an additional source of industrial power. X-energy describes the regulatory decision as the first construction authorization for an advanced nuclear installation at an American industrial location. However, receiving permission to begin construction does not mean the reactors are ready to supply electricity for data centers . Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! The company expects Dow's installation to enter service sometime during the early 2030s, leaving several years before commercial operation begins. The proposed technology uses uranium-bearing fuel pellets, with helium gas circulating through the reactor to carry away generated heat. X-energy argues this arrangement offers safety advantages over conventional nuclear power systems, although independent experts have questioned those assurances. The Union of Concerned Scientists also criticized the regulatory process, particularly the handling of outstanding safety considerations before construction approval. “The NRC only accomplished this feat by pushing consideration of critical safety questions to a later date,” said Edwin Lyman, director of nuclear power safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists. He argued that regulators should have resolved those outstanding concerns before authorizing construction at the industrial location. Demand from artificial intelligence infrastructure operators has given emerging nuclear developers another potential source of commercial interest. Large technology companies need substantial electricity supplies for computing facilities, particularly as increasingly powerful AI systems require additional processing capacity. Conventional electricity providers face growing pressure to accommodate those requirements, creating opportunities for alternative generation technologies. Amazon has become one of X-energy's major financial supporters through its Climate Pledge Fund investment. The technology company led a $500 million Series C-1 financing round in October 2024 and separately committed to purchasing 5 gigawatts of nuclear generating capacity, an agreement which gives X-energy a significant potential customer as it works toward developing commercial reactors. The startup also attracted substantial investor interest through its initial public offering earlier this year, which generated $1 billion in proceeds. However, enthusiasm among investors has moderated since the April listing, suggesting that commercial expectations remain sensitive to development timelines. The company still faces the challenge of turning regulatory permission and financial commitments into functioning electricity-generating infrastructure. Small modular reactors have attracted attention because their developers expect factory-oriented production and smaller installations to simplify construction. Those proposed advantages include shorter development schedules and lower costs, although neither benefit has been conclusively established. No small modular reactor currently operates commercially in the United States, leaving X-energy's proposed installation dependent on successful construction and regulatory oversight. stories.title: Mitra-v2: Scaling synthetic pretraining for tabular foundation models
stories.summary: Expanding the mix of synthetic data used to train a tabular foundation model enables it to adapt to new tables without new models and lead the single-model field on the TabArena benchmark.

sources.name: Amazon Science
sources.title: Mitra-v2: Scaling synthetic pretraining for tabular foundation models
sources.text: Much of the data that businesses run on lives in tables: the rows might represent customers, transactions, or interactions, and their “attributes” are listed in the columns. Predicting missing attributes — such as likelihood of customer retention or how much demand to expect next week — is one of the most common machine learning tasks in industry. The standard tools for this job, such as gradient-boosted decision trees, produce models tailored to specific tables. Every new table means choosing an algorithm, engineering features, tuning hyperparameters, and setting up a processing pipeline. Tabular foundation models promise to end that cycle: one pretrained model reads the labeled rows of a previously unseen table and predicts the rest, with no training run in-between. Last year we introduced Mitra , a tabular foundation model pretrained entirely on synthetic tables. It worked well on small and mid-sized tables but ran out of room on large ones, wide ones, and problems with many classes. Today we're introducing Mitra-v2, the second generation of the model, for both classification and regression. We describe it in a technical report , and we've released versions fine-tuned for both classification and regression, along with the inference and fine-tuning code, under the Apache-2.0 license on Hugging Face. Amazon Connect Customer , which provides agentic-AI systems for core business functions, led the effort. Amazon Connect Customer is adopting Mitra-v2 for prediction on structured business and customer-experience data, such as estimating how likely a business-relevant event is to occur given a customer's interaction history and operational context. On TabArena , a public benchmark of 51 real-world datasets, Mitra-v2 leads the single-model field. It produces a better result than Mitra-v1 on 32 of the 33 datasets where both models run natively, and it completes all 51 datasets within the benchmark's one-hour budget, which Mitra-v1 failed to do on more than a third of them. On ScoringBench , a public benchmark for regression models that predict a range of likely outcomes rather than a single number, fine-tuned Mitra-v2 ranks first. A large language model is pretrained on huge volumes of data, so when you give it a few examples in a prompt, it can generalize from them with no additional training. Tabular foundation models work the same way. We pretrain Mitra-v2 on millions of synthetic prediction problems, and at deployment time the labeled rows of a real table serve as the examples. The model reads them and predicts the unlabeled rows, a technique called in-context learning. Every pretraining table is synthetic: we use no real data, and in particular, no customer data. The model learns general principles about how columns relate to one another rather than the contents of any real dataset. The lesson of the original Mitra was that the quality and diversity of those synthetic tables are central to how well the model generalizes. Mitra-v2 takes that lesson further. The architecture is unchanged: a Transformer that attends both across the rows of a table and across its columns . What has changed is the size of the examples the model sees during pretraining. Mitra-v2 is pretrained on tables with 10 times as many rows and roughly three times as many columns as those used to train Mitra-v1, so it has seen tables the size of the ones businesses actually use. We also added a new family of synthetic tables. To train the original Mitra, we generated tables from structural causal models (SCMs), which are graphs of cause-and-effect relationships between columns, and from tree-based models like the ones data scientists fit in practice. Mitra-v2's new hybrid SCM prior builds a single causal graph in which each relationship can be a small neural network, a decision tree, a smooth function drawn from a Gaussian process, or a time-dependent autoregressive process, so one synthetic table can carry the mix of relationships found in real tables. A new hybrid optimizer keeps training stable across this wider range. At deployment time, two lightweight wrappers extend the model beyond its pretraining limits. For very wide tables, we use singular-value decomposition to produce a new table that fits in the allotted space, populated with synthetic values that capture most of the variance in the original data. Mitra-v2’s output layer has only 10 nodes, corresponding to 10 classes, so for tasks with more classes than that, we send each node’s output toa a hierarchical tree, which further refines the classification. By default, Mitra-v2 is briefly, automatically fine-tuned on each new table it sees, producing eight copies whose predictions are averaged, a standard technique called bagging. So it isn't quite a zero-shot model. The adaptation adds some computational overhead, but in return, it delivers higher accuracy and gives customers additional options. We evaluated Mitra-v2 on TabArena, a living benchmark maintained by an independent academic team. TabArena ranks methods by Elo, the rating system used in chess, here computed from head-to-head wins across datasets under a fixed one-hour budget. Mitra-v2 leads the single-model field, as shown below, with large gains over Mitra-v1 on both classification and regression. It also ranks among the leading methods on the independent TALENT benchmark of roughly 300 datasets, where it's strongest on classification tasks with more than 10 classes. Full results, including per-dataset comparisons, are in the technical report. For regression, Mitra-v2 predicts a full range of likely values for each row rather than a single number, so users get prediction intervals along with the point estimate. That’s the approach that ScoringBench evaluates, rewarding forecasts that are both accurate and well calibrated. On the ScoringBench leaderboard, fine-tuned Mitra-v2 again ranks first.
